controls.title: Accelerator console
readout.title: Readouts
hint.energy.what: Energy of each proton. Injection from the SPS delivers 450 GeV; the RF cavities then raise it by about 5 GeV per second. The collision energy √s is twice the beam energy.
hint.field.what: The dipole magnets keep the protons on the ring. Their field must grow with the momentum: p = 0.2998 · B · ρ, where p is the momentum, B the field and ρ the bending radius. In Auto mode the field follows the energy by itself. In Manual mode you drive it, and if it falls behind, the orbit shifts and the beam hits the wall.
hint.timeSpeed.what: How much game time passes per real second. The LHC ramp takes about 20 minutes, while collecting statistics for rare particles takes months.
hint.sqrtS.what: Hitting a fixed target wastes almost all the energy on moving the centre of mass, so √s grows only as the square root of the beam energy. Colliding beams give everything: √s = 2E. That is why the LHC is a collider.
footer.sources: Machine parameters: LHC Design Report. Masses: Particle Data Group.
beam.title: Beam and luminosity
beam.notColliding: No collisions: the beam must not be ramping
hint.bunches.what: How many proton bunches circulate in each beam. Luminosity grows linearly with the number of bunches. The LHC holds up to 2808 bunches spaced 25 ns apart.
hint.protons.what: How many protons each bunch contains. Luminosity grows with the square of this number, because every proton can hit every other. The design value is 1.15·10¹¹.
hint.betaStar.what: How hard the quadrupole magnets squeeze the beam at the collision point. Smaller β* means a smaller beam spot and more collisions. The design value is 0.55 m; Run 2 reached 0.25 m.
analysis.title: Analysis: μ⁺μ⁻ invariant mass
analysis.resetNote: Changing the pT threshold resets the data, like a new run with a different trigger.
hint.histogram.what: For every pair of muons the detector measures the momenta and we compute the invariant mass: the mass of a particle that could have decayed into them. Random pairs give a smooth background; a real particle gives a peak at its mass.
hint.window.what: Count the events inside a mass window: that is S + B, signal plus background. Estimate the background B from two sidebands of the same total width, assuming it falls smoothly between them. Subtract it to get the signal S. The significance S/√B says how many times the signal exceeds the random scatter of the background. Five sigma counts as a discovery.
hint.ptCut.what: Muons with low transverse momentum never reach the muon chambers, and a low threshold lets in many random pairs. A high threshold kills the light particles: a J/ψ gives muons of only 1.5 GeV each.
tutorial.title: Tutorial
tutorial.lockedKnob: This control unlocks in a later level
cond.windowOnZ: Mass window around 91 GeV, at most 40 GeV wide
level.first-beam.title: First beam
level.first-beam.intro: Protons arrive from the SPS at 450 GeV. To keep them off the wall, the dipole magnets must produce exactly the field that matches their momentum: p = 0.2998 · B · ρ, where p is the proton momentum in GeV/c, B the magnet field in tesla, ρ the bending radius in metres, and 0.2998 a conversion factor. The LHC bending radius is 2804 m.
level.first-beam.goal: Set the dipole field, inject the beam and keep it circulating for 10 seconds.
level.first-beam.hint: The required field is shown in the Readouts panel. Missing by even one per cent shifts the orbit by two centimetres, and the pipe half-width is only 17 mm.
level.first-beam.card: On 10 September 2008 the first proton beam went all the way round the 27 km LHC ring less than an hour after start-up. Nine days later a faulty connection between two magnets caused a helium explosion, and repairs took over a year.
level.ramp.title: Ramp
level.ramp.intro: After injection the RF cavities raise the proton energy. In a synchrotron the orbit radius is fixed, so the magnetic field must grow with the momentum. In Auto mode the system drives the field for you.
level.ramp.goal: Answer the question and ramp the beam to 7 TeV.
level.ramp.hint: The ramp takes about 20 minutes of machine time. Raise the time speed so you do not have to wait.
level.ramp.card: The real ramp takes about 20 minutes: the current in the 1232 superconducting dipoles rises to 11,850 amperes along a precomputed curve. At 8.33 T the magnets hold 7 TeV, and the force trying to burst the coils reaches hundreds of tonnes per metre.
quiz.field-at-7tev.q: What dipole field will 7 TeV need? 450 GeV needs 0.54 T.
level.why-collider.title: Why a collider
level.why-collider.intro: One could accelerate a single beam and fire it at a fixed target. But what matters for producing particles is not the beam energy E but the centre-of-mass energy √s. For a fixed target √s = √(2·m·E), where m is the mass of the target proton: almost all the energy goes into moving the centre of mass. For colliding beams √s = 2E, everything is available.
level.why-collider.goal: Ramp the beam, look at the √s readouts and answer two questions.
level.why-collider.hint: Both values are shown in the Readouts panel while a beam circulates.
level.why-collider.card: The first hadron collider, the ISR, started at CERN in 1971. To reach 14 TeV on a fixed target you would need a 100,000 TeV beam, 15,000 times more energetic than the LHC.
quiz.fixed-target.q: A 7 TeV beam hits a proton at rest. How much energy is available to create particles?
quiz.collider.q: And for two colliding 7 TeV beams?
level.luminosity.title: Luminosity
level.luminosity.intro: Luminosity L measures how densely the beams collide: how many particles pass through a unit area at the collision point per second. The cross section σ is fixed by nature, it is the probability of a process expressed as an area. The number of events is up to us: N = σ · L · t, where t is the running time. Luminosity grows linearly with the number of bunches, with the square of the protons per bunch, and inversely with the focusing β*.
level.luminosity.goal: Answer the question and raise the collision luminosity to 5·10³³ cm⁻²·s⁻¹.
level.luminosity.hint: The beam starts weak. All three knobs in the Beam and luminosity panel work together, and collisions only happen while the beam is not ramping.
level.luminosity.card: The design luminosity of 10³⁴ was reached in June 2016 and doubled during Run 2. The HL-LHC project aims for 5·10³⁴ with new focusing magnets and crab cavities.
level.first-peak.title: First peak
level.first-peak.intro: The detector measures the muon momenta and we compute the invariant mass of every pair. Random pairs give a smooth background; a real particle that decayed into two muons gives a peak at its mass.
level.first-peak.goal: Find the peak, put the mass window on it and collect 500 signal events at 5σ. Then name the particle's mass.
level.first-peak.hint: The peak shows even at injection energy. Zoom the range and move the window so the peak sits inside and the sidebands sit on the background.
level.first-peak.card: The J/ψ was discovered in November 1974 by two groups at once: Samuel Ting's at Brookhaven and Burton Richter's at SLAC. It turned out to be a bound pair of charm quarks, and the November Revolution confirmed the quark model.
quiz.peak-mass.q: What is the mass of the particle behind the peak?
level.z-boson.title: Z boson
level.z-boson.intro: Heavy particles are rare and need energy. The Z production cross section at injection energy is 16 times smaller than at 13 TeV. And a low pT threshold lets in a lot of background.
level.z-boson.goal: Find the Z boson peak: a window around 91 GeV, 100 signal events and 5σ.
level.z-boson.hint: Ramp the beam, raise the muon pT threshold to remove background, and pick the 60–120 range.
level.z-boson.card: The Z boson was discovered in 1983 at CERN's SppS collider: the UA1 and UA2 experiments each saw a handful of events. Carlo Rubbia and Simon van der Meer received the Nobel Prize for it in 1984.
level.sandbox.title: Sandbox
level.sandbox.intro: Every control is open and there are no goals. Try the manual field mode during a ramp, or find the Υ and its excited states.
level.sandbox.hint: Every knob has a hint with a link to its source.
level.sandbox.card: The real LHC collects about 50 fb⁻¹ per year at 13 TeV, and analysing one channel takes a collaboration months.
tutorial.budgetExceeded: Luminosity budget exhausted. Raise the energy, the luminosity or tune the pT threshold, and try again.
hint.channel.what: The same Higgs boson can be searched for through different decay products. The γγ channel: a photon pair, frequent but on a huge background. The 4ℓ channel: four leptons via two Z bosons, almost background-free but only a handful of events.
level.higgs-gammagamma.title: Needle in a haystack
level.higgs-gammagamma.intro: The Higgs boson decays to two photons only twice in a thousand times, while photon pairs are produced in collisions all the time. The peak at 125 GeV barely rises above a smoothly falling background. Statistics decide everything here: the signal grows in proportion to the collected luminosity L·t, while the random scatter of the background grows only as its square root, so with time the signal climbs out of the noise.
level.higgs-gammagamma.goal: In the γγ channel find the bump at 125 GeV: a window at most 10 GeV wide, 100 signal events and 5σ. Budget: 30 fb⁻¹.
level.higgs-gammagamma.hint: At 13–14 TeV the cross section is three times larger than at 7 TeV. A narrow ±4 GeV window catches almost all the signal and less background. A pT threshold around 30 GeV removes soft pairs.
level.higgs-gammagamma.card: On 4 July 2012 ATLAS and CMS announced the discovery of a new boson with a mass near 125 GeV. In the γγ channel ATLAS had 4.5σ from 10 fb⁻¹ of 2011–2012 data, and together with the 4ℓ channel reached 5.9σ. Two years earlier, at 7 TeV, there had been only a 2.8σ hint.
quiz.five-sigma.q: Why do physicists demand 5σ for a discovery?
quiz.five-sigma.a: It was agreed at a conference in the 1970s
quiz.five-sigma.b: A background fluctuation that large happens less than once in 3.5 million times
level.four-leptons.title: Four leptons
level.four-leptons.intro: The second golden channel: H → ZZ* → four leptons. Almost no background and a precise mass, but the Higgs boson decays this way only once in eight thousand times. Every event counts here.
level.four-leptons.goal: In the 4ℓ channel collect 20 signal events in a window around 125 GeV at 5σ.
level.four-leptons.hint: The leptons in this channel are soft: keep the pT threshold low. There is a Z peak at 91 GeV here too; do not mistake it for the Higgs.
level.four-leptons.card: At the announcement ATLAS had 13 four-lepton events over a background of four, and CMS about the same. Fifty years after the prediction, Peter Higgs and François Englert received the 2013 Nobel Prize.
quiz.why-so-few.q: Why are there so few events in the 4ℓ channel?
quiz.why-so-few.a: The Higgs boson is produced less often than the Z
quiz.why-so-few.c: The Higgs decays to four leptons only once in eight thousand times
explainer.beam.title: The beam
explainer.beam.lede: The beam is not a jet but a train of short proton bunches circling the ring at almost the speed of light. Each knob on the panel changes one of three things: how many cars the train has, how many protons ride in each car, and how tightly they are squeezed at the collision point.
explainer.beam.bunches.title: Bunches
explainer.beam.bunches.text: Bunches follow each other every {spacing} m, that is every 25 nanoseconds. The ring has room for {slots} such slots, but at most 2808 can be filled: gaps are needed for injection and for dumping the beam. More bunches mean more crossings of the two trains, and luminosity grows linearly.
explainer.beam.bunch.title: One bunch
explainer.beam.bunch.text: A bunch about 7.5 cm long and as thin as a hair holds a hundred billion protons. When two bunches meet they pass through each other, and of all the possible pairs only a few or a few dozen actually collide. The number of collisions per crossing grows with the square of the protons per bunch.
explainer.beam.focus.title: Focusing β*
explainer.beam.focus.text: Before the collision point quadrupole magnets squeeze the beam like a lens squeezes light. The smaller β*, the narrower the waist, but the faster the beam flares out on either side. The beam size at the waist follows from the focusing and the emittance by the formula below.
explainer.beam.luminosity.title: Luminosity
explainer.beam.luminosity.text: Luminosity measures how densely the beams collide: how many particles pass through a unit area at the collision point per second. It puts everything together: protons squared, number of bunches, revolution frequency and the spot area. Multiply it by a cross section and by time and you get the number of events. That is why rare particles need not only energy but months of running.
explainer.magnets.title: Ring and magnets
explainer.magnets.lede: In a synchrotron the protons follow the same ring at every energy. So the magnetic field must match the momentum exactly: too weak and the protons drift outward, too strong and they drift inward.
explainer.magnets.bend.title: Bending in a dipole
explainer.magnets.bend.text: {dipoles} superconducting dipoles bend the path on a radius of {radius} m. Momentum, field and radius are tied by the formula below: 450 GeV needs 0.54 T, 7 TeV needs 8.33 T. During the ramp the field rises in step with the energy.
explainer.magnets.orbit.title: Mismatch and aperture
explainer.magnets.orbit.text: If the field does not match the momentum, the closed orbit shifts. The beam pipe has a half-width of {aperture} mm, so with a dispersion of {dispersion} m a mismatch of even one per cent puts the protons into the wall.
explainer.mass.title: Invariant mass
explainer.mass.lede: A heavy particle lives far too briefly to reach the detector. We only see its decay products. But energy and momentum are conserved, so the parent's mass can be computed from what is left.
explainer.mass.decay.title: What the detector sees
explainer.mass.decay.text: A particle X is produced in the collision and decays at once. Charged products leave tracks bent by the detector's magnetic field: the radius of curvature is proportional to the transverse momentum. That is how each track's momentum is measured, and the track type tells the particle.
explainer.mass.formula.title: The formula
explainer.mass.formula.text: Add up the energies of the products and add their momenta as vectors. The difference of the squares does not depend on how X was moving and equals the square of its mass. For a random pair of tracks with no common parent this quantity takes any value.
explainer.mass.peak.title: Why a peak appears
explainer.mass.peak.text: Random pairs give a smooth background. Pairs from a real particle give the same mass every time, and a peak grows on the histogram. Its width is the detector resolution plus the particle's own width, and its height above the background grows with the collected luminosity.
sym.const: conversion factor so that momentum is in GeV/c, field in tesla and radius in metres
sym.dx: closed-orbit offset from the pipe axis
sym.D: dispersion: how far the orbit moves for a 100 % momentum error
sym.dpp: relative momentum error compared with what the field holds
sym.L: luminosity: how many particles pass through a unit area at the collision point per second
sym.N: protons in one bunch (squared, because every proton of one bunch can meet every proton of the other)
sym.frev: revolution frequency: how many times per second a bunch passes the collision point
sym.sigma: transverse beam size at the collision point
sym.4pi: spot area: two round Gaussian beams of size σ give an effective area of 4πσ²
sym.eps: emittance: the beam's volume in phase space, shrinks as the energy grows
sym.betastar: focusing strength: the distance from the collision point at which the beam is twice as wide again
sym.Nev: number of events of the process of interest
sym.sigmaX: cross section of the process: the probability that a collision produces it, expressed as an area (1 barn = 10⁻²⁴ cm²)
sym.intL: luminosity times the running time, the integrated luminosity (in fb⁻¹)
sym.m: mass of the particle X that decayed
sym.E1E2: energies of the decay products as measured by the detector
sym.p1p2: momenta of the products, added as vectors
hint.luminosity.what: Luminosity measures how densely the beams collide: how many particles pass through a unit area at the collision point per second. The number of events of any process is its cross section times the luminosity times the time. The unit cm⁻²·s⁻¹: 10³⁴ means a process with a 1 nb (10⁻³³ cm²) cross section gives 10 events per second.
